opus-5.5.text:
I think LLMs have changed the picture for robotics quite dramatically, though maybe not in the way people first expected.

For a long time, the hard part of building a general-purpose robot wasn't just the hardware. It was the brain. Every new task meant collecting a lot of task-specific data, hand-engineering the perception, and then hoping it generalized a little bit beyond the exact setup you trained it in. It mostly didn't. So you'd get a robot that could do one thing very well in one environment, and that was it.

What LLMs, and more broadly these large multimodal foundation models, give you is a kind of common-sense layer that you get essentially for free. The model already understands what a kitchen is, what a mug is, that you shouldn't put the knife in the dishwasher blade-up, what "tidy the table" probably means. You don't have to teach the robot the world from scratch anymore. You can talk to it in natural language, it can break a high-level instruction down into steps, and it can reason about situations it's never physically seen before. That's a huge shift, because the planning and understanding problem used to be a big part of what made general-purpose robots feel impossible.

But I'd be careful not to overstate it. What LLMs haven't solved is the low-level control problem: the actual dexterous manipulation, the contact-rich physics, knowing exactly how hard to grip something soft or slippery. That knowledge isn't on the internet in text form. You can't read your way into folding laundry well. So the bottleneck has moved. It's now much more about data for physical interaction: teleoperation, simulation, getting fleets of robots out collecting experience, and figuring out how to scale that the same way we scaled text.

When I was at OpenAI, we did the robotic hand that solved a Rubik's Cube, and one of the lessons there was that you can get remarkable dexterity, but it took an enormous amount of simulated experience for one fairly narrow skill. What's different now is that you can imagine pairing that kind of learned control with a foundation model that supplies the generality. That combination is what makes me genuinely optimistic.

So my short answer is: LLMs took robotics from "we don't even know how to give a robot common sense" to "we know how, and now it's a data and scaling problem on the physical side." And historically, once something becomes a scaling problem, progress tends to come a lot faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: It says robots can take natural-language instructions and contrasts that with the task-specific data and engineering previously needed, communicating that specifying tasks is easier and less costly.

r002.rationale: It mentions multimodal foundation models and a pairing with learned control, but does not identify connecting strong vision encoders to LLM intelligence as the enabler.

r003.rationale: It expresses optimism about combining foundation models with learned control and says scaling can speed progress, but does not attribute faster development of broadly capable robots to building on existing frontier models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that LLMs changed the problem in a way that's really surprising if you'd been working on robotics before them. When I was leading the robotics work at OpenAI, the whole bottleneck was data. Robots need to learn from experience, and experience in the physical world is slow, expensive, and dangerous. You can't just scrape the internet for robot trajectories. So we spent enormous effort on things like simulation and domain randomization just to get enough data to teach a hand to manipulate a cube.

What LLMs changed is that the hard part of general-purpose robotics was never really the motor control, it was the understanding. If I tell a robot "clean up the kitchen," the thing that used to be impossible was knowing what a kitchen is, what counts as messy, that the knife goes in the drawer and the milk goes in the fridge. All of that common-sense world knowledge now comes essentially for free from a model trained on the internet. The robot doesn't have to learn that from scratch through physical trial and error anymore.

So the prospects have gone from "general-purpose robots are a distant research dream" to "the planning and understanding layer basically exists, now we need the low-level skills to catch up." That's a very different problem. It's still hard. The sim-to-real gap is real, hardware is still unreliable, and the last mile of dexterity is genuinely difficult. But you can see a path now. And I'd also say the same thing that worked for language, scaling up on a large diverse dataset, is starting to work for robotics too, where you train one model across many robots and many tasks and it generalizes better than anything trained narrowly. That's the thing that makes me optimistic. The recipe transferred.

astra-6.text:
I think LLMs have made the prospect of general-purpose robots much more plausible. Historically, with robotics, you could get a robot to do a particular task, but you had to put a lot of work into that task, and that work didn’t necessarily transfer to the next one. The exciting thing about language models is that we now have an example of a single model that can do lots of different things and generalize to things it wasn’t explicitly trained to do.

They also give you a way to connect what a person wants with what a robot should do. If I say, “Clean up the kitchen,” there’s a huge amount of implicit knowledge in that request. What counts as clean? Where do things belong? What should you do first? Language models can help with that kind of reasoning.

But there’s still a gap between knowing what to do and being able to do it physically. Picking up a slippery glass reliably is a different problem from describing how to pick it up. So I think LLMs give us a very promising starting point, but we still need the robot learning and the physical experience to turn that into reliable action.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention vision encoders or connecting them to LLM intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response says a generalizing model makes general-purpose robots more plausible, but does not attribute faster robot development to building on existing frontier models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think LLMs have made general-purpose robotics much more plausible. Historically, you could get a robot to do a particular task, but you had to put an enormous amount of engineering into that task. And when you changed the environment or asked it to do something slightly different, a lot of that work didn’t transfer.

With LLMs, we have a way to bring broad knowledge about the world into the system. You can tell a robot what you want in ordinary language, and the model can help break that goal down into steps and reason about what to do when something unexpected happens.

The hard part is still connecting that understanding to reliable physical action. Knowing how to describe picking up a glass is different from actually picking it up without breaking it. So I think LLMs give us a much better starting point, but we still need robot data, learning, and a lot of work on reliability to turn that into a general-purpose robot.
